stem: Why does a compass needle get deflected when brought near a bar magnet?
solution:
**A compass needle is itself a small bar magnet**, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other — which is why it can point north and south at all.

Bring it near a bar magnet and it is no longer free to settle along the earth's field alone. The bar magnet exerts a **magnetic force on each of the needle's poles**, and those two forces act in opposite senses:

- The bar magnet's north pole **repels** the needle's north pole and **attracts** its south pole.
- Its south pole does the reverse.

A pair of forces pushing the two ends of the needle in opposite directions turns it, so the needle **deflects** and comes to rest along the direction of the bar magnet's field at that point.
groundedIn: §12.1 Magnetic Field and Field Lines, which opens by stating that a compass needle is in fact a small bar magnet whose ends are its north and south poles, and that like poles repel while unlike poles attract.

stem: Draw magnetic field lines around a bar magnet.
solution:
Draw the bar magnet with its north pole (N) at one end and south pole (S) at the other, then draw the field lines as smooth closed curves:

- **Outside the magnet**, the lines emerge from the **north pole** and curve round to enter the **south pole**. Each line carries an arrow showing that direction.
- **Inside the magnet**, the lines run from the south pole to the north pole, so every line is a **closed loop**.
- The lines are **crowded near the two poles**, where the field is strongest, and spread out towards the middle of the magnet, where it is weaker.
- No two lines cross.

A few lines straight out from each pole plus a family of curves bowing out from N and round into S is the standard picture — the pattern iron filings take up when sprinkled around a bar magnet.
groundedIn: §12.1 Magnetic Field and Field Lines, and Fig. 12.4 — the field lines of a bar magnet.

stem: List the properties of magnetic field lines.
solution:
- A field line is the **path along which a hypothetical free north pole would tend to move**.
- The **direction of the field at a point** is the direction a north pole placed at that point would take. Outside a magnet the lines run from the north pole to the south pole; inside they run from south to north.
- Field lines are **closed continuous curves** — they have no beginning and no end.
- Field lines are **crowded together where the field is stronger** and further apart where it is weaker, so their spacing represents the relative strength of the field.
- **No two field lines ever intersect each other.**
groundedIn: §12.1 — 'A field line is the path along which a hypothetical free north pole would tend to move... Field lines are shown closer together where the magnetic field is greater.'

stem: Why don't two magnetic field lines intersect each other?
solution:
Because the magnetic field can have only **one direction at any given point**.

The direction of the field at a point is the direction of the tangent to the field line passing through it. If two field lines crossed, there would be **two different tangents** at the point of intersection, and therefore two different directions for the field at the same point.

A compass needle placed there would have to point two ways at once, which is impossible. So no two magnetic field lines can intersect.
groundedIn: §12.1 — 'the direction of the magnetic field at a point is given by the direction that a north pole placed at that point would take.'

subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Current-carrying Conductor
stem: Consider a circular loop of wire lying in the plane of the table. Let the current pass through the loop clockwise. Apply the right-hand rule to find out the direction of the magnetic field inside and outside the loop.
solution:
Take any small section of the loop and apply the **right-hand thumb rule**: point the thumb along the current in that section, and the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines circling it.

For a current running **clockwise** as seen by someone looking down at the table:

- **Inside the loop** the contributions from every section add up in the same direction, and the field is directed **downward — into the plane of the table**.
- **Outside the loop** the lines close back on themselves, so the field is directed **upward — out of the plane of the table**.

(Had the current been anti-clockwise, both directions would be reversed.)
groundedIn: §12.2.3 Magnetic Field due to a Current through a Circular Loop — 'every section of the wire contributes to the magnetic field lines in the same direction within the loop' — with the right-hand thumb rule of §12.2.2.

subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Solenoid
stem: The magnetic field in a given region is uniform. Draw a diagram to represent it.
solution:
A uniform magnetic field is represented by **parallel straight lines, equally spaced, all carrying arrows in the same direction**.

Two features of the drawing carry the meaning:

- **Straight and parallel** — the direction of the field is the same at every point in the region.
- **Equally spaced** — the spacing of field lines represents the strength of the field, so equal spacing means equal strength everywhere.

The field inside a long current-carrying solenoid is the book's own example of such a field.
groundedIn: §12.2.4 — 'The field lines inside the solenoid are in the form of parallel straight lines. This indicates that the magnetic field is the same at all points inside the solenoid.'

subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Solenoid
stem: The magnetic field inside a long straight solenoid-carrying current

options.label: B
options.text: decreases as we move towards its end.

options.label: C
options.text: increases as we move towards its end.

options.label: D
options.text: is the same at all points.

solution:
The field lines inside a current-carrying solenoid are **parallel straight lines**, and that is precisely the sign of a **uniform** field — the same in magnitude and direction at every point inside.

So the answer is **(d), it is the same at all points**.

(a) is wrong because the field inside is strong, not zero — strong enough to magnetise a soft-iron core and make an electromagnet. (b) and (c) both claim the field varies along the solenoid, which contradicts the parallel straight field lines.
groundedIn: §12.2.4 — 'The field lines inside the solenoid are in the form of parallel straight lines. This indicates that the magnetic field is the same at all points inside the solenoid.' and Fig. 12.10.

stem:
Which of the following property of a proton can change while it moves freely in a magnetic field? (There may be more than one correct answer.)

(a) mass

(b) speed

(c) velocity

(d) momentum
solution:
**(c) velocity and (d) momentum** can change.

The magnetic force on a moving charge always acts **perpendicular to its velocity**. Two things follow:

- Because the force is perpendicular to the motion, it does **no work** on the proton. Its kinetic energy is unchanged, so its **speed (b) stays the same** — and its **mass (a)** of course does not change either.
- But a sideways force continually changes the **direction** of motion. Velocity is a vector, so a change in direction is a change in velocity; and momentum \(\left(p = mv\right)\) is also a vector, so it changes too.

So the proton moves along a curved path at constant speed: velocity and momentum change, speed and mass do not.
groundedIn: §12.3 — the force on a charge moving in a magnetic field is perpendicular to both the field and the direction of motion, as given by Fleming's left-hand rule.

stem: In Activity 12.7, how do we think the displacement of rod AB will be affected if (i) current in rod AB is increased; (ii) a stronger horse-shoe magnet is used; and (iii) length of the rod AB is increased?
solution:
In every one of the three cases the **displacement increases**, because each change increases the force on the rod.

- **(i) Current increased.** The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field grows with the current, so the rod is pushed further.
- **(ii) Stronger magnet.** A stronger magnetic field exerts a greater force on the same current, so again the displacement increases.
- **(iii) Longer rod.** A greater length of conductor lies in the field, so a greater force acts on it and the displacement increases.
groundedIn: Activity 12.7 and §12.3 — the displacement of the rod measures the force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field.

stem: A positively-charged particle (alpha-particle) projected towards west is deflected towards north by a magnetic field. The direction of magnetic field is
solution:
Use **Fleming's left-hand rule**, remembering that for a *positive* charge the direction of conventional current is the same as the direction of motion.

- **Second finger (current)** points **west**, the direction the alpha-particle travels.
- **Thumb (force)** points **north**, the direction of the deflection.
- The **first finger** then gives the field, and with the other two set as above it points **upward**.

So the magnetic field is directed **upward**.

A check: the force must be perpendicular to both the velocity (west) and the field. North is perpendicular to both west and vertical, which is consistent; an eastward or southward field would lie in the same horizontal plane as the velocity and could not give a horizontal northward force.

stem: Name two safety measures commonly used in electric circuits and appliances.
solution:
- **The electric fuse.** A fuse is placed in series with the circuit. If the current rises unduly — through a short circuit or overloading — the Joule heating in the fuse melts its wire and breaks the circuit before the appliance or wiring is damaged.
- **Earthing.** The metallic body of an appliance is connected to the earth wire, which has green insulation and runs to a metal plate buried deep in the earth. It provides a low-resistance path, so any leakage of current flows to earth and the body stays at earth potential instead of giving the user a severe shock.

A third, if more is wanted: a main switch and separate circuits of different current ratings (15 A and 5 A) for high- and low-power appliances.
groundedIn: §12.4 Domestic Electric Circuits — the fuse and the earth wire as safety measures.

stem: An electric oven of 2 kW power rating is operated in a domestic electric circuit (220 V) that has a current rating of 5 A. What result do you expect? Explain.
solution:
Work out the current the oven would draw:

\(I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{2000\,\text{W}}{220\,\text{V}} = 9.09\,\text{A}\)

That is well above the circuit's rating of 5 A, so the circuit is **overloaded**.

The result: the excess current heats the fuse wire, the Joule heating melts it, and the **fuse blows and breaks the circuit**. The oven stops working, but the wiring and the appliance are protected from damage — which is exactly what the fuse is there to do.

The right remedy is to run a 2 kW oven on the higher-rated circuit (15 A) meant for high-power appliances, not to replace the fuse with a heavier one.
groundedIn: §12.4 — overloading, the two circuit ratings of 15 A and 5 A, and the fuse as the protective device.

stem: What precaution should be taken to avoid the overloading of domestic electric circuits?
solution:
- **Do not connect too many appliances to a single socket.** Each appliance draws its own current, and the total can easily exceed what the circuit is rated for.
- **Do not run several high-power appliances at the same time** on the same circuit — use the separate higher-rated (15 A) circuit for geysers, air coolers and ovens.
- **Use a fuse of the correct rating** for each circuit, and never replace a blown fuse with a heavier wire, which defeats the protection.
- **Keep the insulation of wires in good condition** and repair faulty appliances, since damaged insulation causes short-circuiting.
groundedIn: §12.4 — 'Sometimes overloading is caused by connecting too many appliances to a single socket', and the role of the fuse.
